shell.reloadClashes: Read again. Another administrator changed the same field, so it shows their value — what you entered here: {{values}}
shell.reloadClashesHidden: Read again. Another administrator changed the same field, so it shows their value. Enter your change again.

email.title: SMTP email delivery
email.meta: Set up the mail this server sends.
email.signupInvitedHelp: People with an invitation, from a workspace’s allowed email domains, or logging in with your organization’s SSO can create accounts. Others see that sign-up is closed.
email.signupPublicHelp: Anyone who can reach this server can create an account.
email.signupContactHelp: Shown as written to people who find sign-up closed, or who can’t sign up because the server couldn’t send its email, such as an email address or team name. Leave empty to show none.
email.memberAddHelp: Sets whether existing server accounts can be newly added to workspaces. Changing or removing existing members is not affected.
email.secretHelp: Secret values are never shown again and are replaced only when you enter a new value.
email.useSmtpBody: Sends account confirmations, password resets, invitations and notifications.
email.requireVerificationBody: Asks new accounts to confirm their address by mail.
email.senderInvalid: Enter the address mail is sent from, like noreply@example.com.
email.passwordRequired: Enter the password for this user name. For a server that needs no login, leave the user name empty.
email.noSignInHint: For a server that needs no login (a relay on this machine or network), leave the user name and password empty.
email.switcherListsHelp: People can let their other Leafen servers’ pages list their workspaces and apps here (names and icons only) in the workspace switcher.
email.verificationNeedsSmtp: To turn SMTP off, first turn off “Require email verification for signup” above. Email verification needs SMTP.

providers.meta: Who can create an account and join workspaces, and how people log in.
providers.issuerUnusable: No usable OpenID settings were found at this issuer address. Check the address and that the provider is running, then save again.
providers.redirectHint: Add this redirect URI to the OAuth client you create at the provider.
providers.redirectLocal: Only this computer opens this address. For others to log in, turn on Access from outside first.
providers.redirectUnknown: The server’s address couldn’t be read, so the redirect URI can’t be shown.
providers.returnMoved: The server’s address changed. Add the new redirect URI below to the provider’s OAuth client; until then, logins go through the earlier address {{earlier}}, which forwards here.
providers.returnAdded: Logins now use the new redirect URI, and this note disappears after the first one succeeds. If the provider rejects it, switch back to the earlier address.
providers.returnUndo: Switch back to the earlier address
providers.googleClientIdRequired: Enter the client ID of your Google OAuth client.
providers.googleSecretRequired: Enter the client secret of your Google OAuth client.
providers.oidcNameRequired: Enter the name people see on the login button.
providers.oidcClientIdRequired: Enter the client ID from your provider
providers.oidcSecretRequired: Enter the client secret from your provider
providers.oidcScopesRequired: Include openid in the scopes, separated by spaces
providers.issuerRequired: Enter your provider’s address, like https://login.example.com.

users.title: Server users
users.meta: Manage server accounts, login status, and transfers of owned resources.
users.name: Name
users.passwordFieldBody: Leave empty to make a temporary one.
users.joinedViaWorkspaceEmail: Joined {{when}} via an email invitation to {{workspace}} from {{inviter}}.
users.joinedViaPageEmail: Joined {{when}} via a page {{inviter}} shared by email in {{workspace}}.
users.joinedViaWorkspaceName: Joined {{when}} via an invitation by name to {{workspace}} from {{inviter}}.
users.joinedViaWorkspaceLink: Joined {{when}} via {{workspace}}’s invite link, enabled by {{inviter}}.
users.joinedViaTeamspaceLink: Joined {{when}} via a teamspace’s invite link in {{workspace}}, enabled by {{inviter}}.
users.joinedViaAllowedDomain: Joined {{when}} via an email domain allowed by {{workspace}}.
users.joinedViaPageLink: Joined {{when}} via a guest invite link {{inviter}} made in {{workspace}}.
users.confirmRevokeDeviceDetail: That device returns to the login screen immediately
users.disabled: Disabled {{name}} and revoked all its sessions
users.confirmResetDetail: They’re logged out of every browser and must set a new password after logging in with the temporary one.
users.confirmDisableDetail: They’re logged out everywhere and can’t log in until restored.
users.confirmRevokeSessionsNoEmail: They’re logged out of every device at once. With no email to log in with, they log in again with a device code you create here.
users.confirmDisableNoEmail: They’re logged out everywhere and can’t log in until restored. With no email to log in with, they then log in with a device code you create here.
users.confirmRevokeSessionsDetail: They’re logged out on every device at once
users.passwordReset: Made a temporary password for {{name}} and revoked all its sessions.
users.deviceCodeIssued: A device code for {{email}}, for ten minutes and once. Give it to them only: they open the address, or choose “Log in with a code” on the login page and type the code.
users.deviceCodeQRAlt: QR code that logs a device in to the account
users.deviceCodeUsed: A device logged in to {{email}} with the code. It can’t be used again.
users.deviceCodeExpired: The device code for {{email}} expired after ten minutes. Create another if they still need one.
users.confirmDeleteDetail: If it owns resources, choose their new owners first.
users.deleted: Deleted {{name}} and transferred what it owned
users.chooseOwners: Choose a new owner for each owned resource.
users.actionFailed: Couldn’t complete the server user action
users.changedMeanwhile: This account changed elsewhere in the meantime, so the list was read again. Check it and try again.
users.cleanupChooseNote: Choose who takes over what this account owns. The account is deleted after that.

backup.title: Backup file
backup.meta: Creates a complete Leafen server backup including login data and files.
backup.help: Backups are kept for 7 days. Restore runs from the CLI into an empty Leafen data root, using the downloaded file and the SHA-256 shown.
backup.replayed: The existing backup request was checked again
backup.checked: Checked the current state of the backup request
backup.failedHelp: The backup couldn’t be made. Check that the server can write to its data folder and that the disk has room, then try again.
backup.failedNoSpace: The disk had no room for the backup file. Free some space, then try again.
backup.failedBusy: Another backup or restore was running, so the backup file wasn’t made. Try again once it ends.
backup.phase_snapshot: Taking a snapshot of the data
backup.restoreWay_server: In the folder holding this file, the command below restores it into a new data folder, leafen-restored. Once it reports “restored”, stop this server and start it on that folder (serve --dir=leafen-restored).
backup.restoreWay_container: Put this file in the folder holding compose.yaml, stop the server with docker compose down and remove its data volume (…_leafen-data in docker volume ls). Then, in that folder, restore with the command below and start it with docker compose up -d.
backup.restoreWay_app: This file is restored on a computer where the Leafen app has never been opened. Install the app and, before opening it, run the command below in a terminal in the folder holding this file, then open the app.
backup.restoreWay_phone: A phone has no terminal to run a command, so this file is restored on a computer. Move it to a computer with Leafen, and that Leafen’s Backups → “Restoring from this file” gives the command to run there. To move this phone’s Leafen to another server whole, use Restore and move → “Move this server”, which needs no file.

identity.name: Server name
identity.nameMeta: Agents and apps on other servers tell this server apart by this name. If empty, it’s {{alias}}. Agent connection names and the public address already made stay as they are.
identity.title: Server number
identity.meta: This server’s own number. It stays the same through backups, restores and moves of its data.

updates.title: Version
updates.dockerWay: This server runs in Docker. Installed with Docker Compose, update it in the folder of compose.yaml: docker compose pull, then docker compose up -d. On a NAS, Container Manager or Portainer does the same by pulling the image again and making the container again (a project’s Build, a stack’s re-pull and redeploy). The data, settings and connections stay, and the server keeps the data from before as it updates.
updates.checkOff: Checking for a newer version is off
updates.checkFailed: Couldn’t check for a new version. It will try again later
updates.notChecked: Not checked for a newer version yet
updates.checkHelp: Once a day, asks whether the signed release information (latest version, security flag, sponsor list) changed and fetches it when it did. No workspace, account, or usage information is sent. Sponsorships fund Leafen development.
updates.checkEnvironmentOff: Checking is turned off by the server environment variable LEAFEN_UPDATE_CHECK=off, so only the information bundled with the release is used.
updates.appAutoUpdateHelp: Downloads a newer version in the background, verifies who made it, and switches when the app restarts. A copy of the data is kept, and a version that fails to start rolls back to the previous one.
updates.appAutoUpdateManaged: Your organization turned updating off for this app (LEAFEN_DESKTOP_AUTO_UPDATE=off).
updates.meta: This server’s version, and checking for new ones.
updates.securityBand: Security update {{version}} is out. Update this server.

map.title: Map background
map.meta: Chooses the map drawn under the pins of database map views.
map.privacy: With external maps on, the browser of whoever opens a map view requests tiles straight from the tile server, which passes that person’s IP address and this server’s address (origin) to the tile provider (the OpenStreetMap Foundation by default). Off, or when tiles can’t be loaded, only the bundled Natural Earth outline is drawn. An API key in the tile address is visible to everyone who opens a map.
map.environmentOff: External maps are turned off by the server environment variable LEAFEN_MAP_TILES_DISABLED, so only the bundled outline is shown whatever the settings below say.
map.otherServers: For another tile server, enter an address with {z}, {x} and {y} placeholders together with the attribution its provider requires.

schedule.title: Scheduled backups
schedule.meta: Back this server up to a folder, a WebDAV server or S3-compatible storage you choose, on a schedule.
schedule.help: Choose a cloud drive’s synced folder, a NAS share or an external disk to keep the backups somewhere else too. A backup holds the server’s secret keys too, so choose a folder others can’t read.
schedule.helpContainer: This server runs in a container, so it can’t write to a folder path of this computer. Enter {{folder}}, the place mounted for backups, or a folder in it. A backup holds the server’s secret keys too, so keep it where others can’t read it.
schedule.helpDevice: Choose a cloud drive’s folder to keep the backups even if this phone is lost. A backup holds the server’s secret keys too, so choose a folder others can’t read.
schedule.savedStarted: Saved the backup schedule. A backup starts now
schedule.alreadyRunning: Already backing up; nothing new was started
schedule.startsOnSave: Saving starts a backup at once.
schedule.setByEnvironment: This server’s environment (LEAFEN_BACKUP_FOLDER, LEAFEN_BACKUP_WEBDAV_URL or LEAFEN_BACKUP_S3_BUCKET) sets its backups.
schedule.folderInvalid: The backup folder must be a full path outside the data folder that the server can write to, in a folder that is already there.
schedule.folderInvalidContainer: This server runs in a container, so it can’t write to that path. Enter {{folder}}, the place mounted for backups, or a folder in it.
schedule.folderInvalidDevice: Couldn’t write to the chosen folder. Choose another one.
schedule.webdavPasswordNone: Leave empty for a server without one
schedule.webdavInsecure: This is an http address, so the WebDAV password travels unencrypted. Use an https address unless the server is on the same network.
schedule.webdavHelp: Give the address of a folder on a WebDAV server such as Nextcloud or Synology. Create an app password rather than using the account’s own.
schedule.webdavInvalid: Couldn’t reach or write to the WebDAV address. Check that the http or https address names a folder and that the server can reach it.
schedule.webdavCredentialsMissing: This WebDAV server asks for a user name and password. Fill in the empty field to back up there.
schedule.s3PathStyle: Use path-style addresses (storage such as MinIO that puts the bucket in the path)
schedule.s3Insecure: This is an http endpoint, so the keys travel unencrypted. Use an https endpoint unless the storage is on the same network.
schedule.s3Help: Backups go to a bucket of S3-compatible storage such as AWS S3, Backblaze B2, Cloudflare R2 or MinIO. Create keys that can access only that bucket.
schedule.s3Invalid: Couldn’t reach or write to the storage. Check the endpoint, region and bucket name, and that the server can reach them.
schedule.s3KeysMissing: Enter both the access key and the secret key to back up to this storage.
schedule.conflict: The backup schedule changed elsewhere. Open it again to check.
schedule.failedFolder: Couldn’t write to the backup folder. Check that it exists and the server can write to it.
schedule.failedFolderDevice: Couldn’t write to the chosen folder. Check that it’s still there, or choose it again.
schedule.failedForeign: This place holds another server’s backups, so this server’s backup wasn’t written there. To restore from them, open them with their recovery code or password in Restore and move. For this server’s backups, choose another place.
schedule.failedOpened: This place holds another server’s backups, opened here, so this server’s backup wasn’t written there. Restore from them, or press “Write here” to write this server’s backups at this place.
schedule.openedMeta: You opened another server’s backups at this place. Until you restore from them, this server writes no backups here, so the number kept never removes them. Writing here counts this server’s backups with them against the number kept.
schedule.failedWebdav: Couldn’t reach or write to the WebDAV server. Check that it’s running and the address is right.
schedule.failedWebdavUnauthorized: The WebDAV server refused access to the backups.
schedule.failedS3: Couldn’t reach or write to the S3 storage. Check that the endpoint and bucket exist.
schedule.failedS3Unauthorized: The S3 storage refused access to the backups.
schedule.failedSpace: The backup folder is out of space.
schedule.failed: Couldn’t back up. Check the server’s log.
schedule.failedMissingFolder: The backup folder isn’t there. Check that it still exists, or choose it again.
schedule.failedMissingWebdav: The WebDAV server has no folder at that address. Check the address.
schedule.failedMissingS3: The storage has no such bucket. Check the bucket name and region.
schedule.failedMovedWebdav: The WebDAV server sent that address somewhere else. Check its path and the / at its end.
schedule.failedMovedS3: The storage sent the request to another address or region. Check the endpoint and region.
schedule.failedUnreachableWebdav: The WebDAV server doesn’t answer. Check that it’s running and that this server can reach its address.
schedule.failedUnreachableS3: The S3 storage doesn’t answer. Check the endpoint and the network.

cause.signIn: Common cause: a wrong user name and password (or keys), or the storage asking to confirm this new device (usually by email) or for an app password.
cause.permission: Common cause: the account has no permission for that folder or bucket.
cause.address: Common cause: the address is missing the / at its end, or the storage wants its own region’s address.
cause.space: Common cause: the storage, or the account’s quota there, is full.

schedule.passwordKept: Set — type a new one to change it
schedule.notice: Scheduled backups failed {{count}} times in a row.
schedule.offNoticeComputer: Scheduled backups are off, so your data is only on this computer.
schedule.offNoticeServer: Scheduled backups are off, so the data is only on this server.
schedule.offNoticeDevice: Scheduled backups are off, so your data is only on this phone.
schedule.syncFoldersHelp: Pick one to back up every day into a Leafen backups folder inside it, keeping the last 7.
schedule.followsPrimary: This server is a standby and follows its primary’s backups.
schedule.enabledMeta: When it’s off, this server’s data is only on this server.
schedule.restoreMeta: Go back to a backup kept at the backup place.

backupProgress.skipped_one: {{count}} file deleted during the backup skipped
backupProgress.skipped_other: {{count}} files deleted during the backup skipped

protection.title: Backup protection
protection.codeShownOnce: This recovery code is shown only now. Copy it, print it or write it down, and keep it somewhere other than this server.
protection.codeHelp: With this code, the backups open on any server even if this one is lost. Without the code or the password, no one can open them — not even us.
protection.passwordHelp: At least 12 characters and not a common one; a short sentence works well. A forgotten password can’t be recovered.
protection.required: Backups that leave this computer — S3, WebDAV or a cloud sync folder — need a recovery code or a password first.
protection.requiredDevice: A backup in a folder chosen on the phone needs a recovery code or a password first.
protection.help: The backups’ data, files and lists are encrypted. Either the recovery code or the password opens them, and changing one doesn’t affect the other or earlier backups.
protection.offHelp: Backups kept on this computer can stay unencrypted. Make a recovery code to encrypt them and to back up off this computer.
protection.offHelpDevice: Make a recovery code to encrypt the backups and keep them in a folder chosen on the phone.
protection.passwordChanged: The backup password is changed. Earlier backups open with it too.
protection.firstSealed: Backups are encrypted from now on
protection.codeReplaced: The new recovery code is saved; the old one no longer opens the backups.
protection.weak: Choose a longer backup password: at least 12 characters, not a common one. A short sentence works well.
protection.last: Backups need a recovery code or a password. Add the other one before removing this one.
protection.openHelp: These backups were encrypted by another server or an earlier key. Their recovery code or password opens them here. If they are another server’s, this server writes no backups here until you restore from them or press “Write here” in Backups.
protection.openerWrong: That recovery code or password doesn’t open these backups.
protection.firstSealedOlder: Backups are encrypted from now on. Those made before stay unencrypted until {{count}} new ones replace them; delete them from the backup location sooner if you like.
protection.passwordAdded: The password is set. It opens the backups as the recovery code does.

requestLog.title: Request log
requestLog.meta: What the server records of the requests it answers, for finding out what went wrong.
requestLog.help: Failed requests, requests that take a second or more, and changes by administrators, logins and setup are always kept. The audit logs are kept apart and aren’t affected.
requestLog.entries_one: {{entries}} entry now · at most {{most}}, the oldest go first
requestLog.entries_other: {{entries}} entries now · at most {{most}}, the oldest go first

readLog.title: Read log
readLog.meta: The server records every page, item and file it gives out — who read what, when and how — for those with full access and the organization’s compliance administrators. Turned off, nothing more is recorded; what was recorded stays.

restore.title: Restore from a backup
restore.meta: Replaces what the server holds now with a backup. What it holds now is kept for 7 days, or until the next backup, so the restore can be undone.
restore.none: There are no backups in the folder yet
restore.confirmBody: Everything on this server goes back to how it was at {{time}}. Changes made since then stay only in the kept copy of the current data, which can be restored for 7 days or until the next backup. People may need to log in again.
restore.restartAutomatic: The server starts again, which takes a moment.
restore.restartManual: It happens when the server or app is next started: close it and open it again.
restore.restarting: The server is restarting. This page reloads when it’s back.
restore.waiting: The backup {{name}} is restored when the server or app is next started.
restore.undoWaiting: What the server held before the restore comes back when the server or app is next started.
restore.failed: The restore of the backup {{name}} couldn’t finish as the server or app started at {{time}}: nothing was restored, and Leafen goes on with what it held before.
restore.undoFailed: Undoing the restore couldn’t finish as the server or app started at {{time}}: Leafen goes on with what it held.
restore.undoBody: The server goes back to what it held just before the restore. What changed after the restore is lost. People may need to log in again.
restore.snapshotUnavailable: That backup can’t be opened, or doesn’t hold what its list says.
restore.earlierLeafen: That backup is from an earlier Leafen, which this version doesn’t open, so this server keeps its data. Move its workspaces over one by one instead: make a new workspace here and start it with “Move from another server”, then paste its code in the earlier Leafen’s workspace settings, under Move this workspace.
restore.newerLeafen: That backup is from a newer Leafen than this server. Update this server first, then restore it.
restore.alreadyWaiting: A restore is already pending until the server restarts.
restore.busy: A backup or restore is running. Try again when it finishes.
restore.undoUnavailable: What the server held before the restore is no longer kept.
restore.restartFailed: Couldn’t restart Leafen. Close the app and open it again.
restore.restartInApp: It finishes when the app starts its server again: press Restart now next, or close the app and open it again.
restore.replicaThis: Continuous replica of this server · last change {{time}}
restore.replicaOtherUnknown: Continuous replica of another server · last change {{time}}
restore.replicaConfirmBody: This server’s data will be replaced by {{name}}, as of its last change. The server that wrote the replica stops accepting changes once it notices, and this server continues from the replica.
restore.pageMeta: Take the server back to a backup, or move it whole to another server.
restore.needsBackup: To restore from a backup, turn on scheduled backups first. The backups kept there show here.
restore.folderWay_server: The command below restores a backup from the backup folder into a new data folder, leafen-restored. Once it reports “restored”, stop this server and start it on that folder (serve --dir=leafen-restored).
restore.folderWay_container: Stop the server with docker compose down and remove its data volume (…_leafen-data in docker volume ls). Then, in the folder holding compose.yaml, restore with the command below and start it with docker compose up -d.
restore.folderWay_app: A backup is restored on a computer where the Leafen app has never been opened. Install the app and, before opening it, run the command below in a terminal, then open the app.
restore.folderWay_phone: A phone has no terminal to run a command, so a backup is restored on this screen, chosen from the list above. If the app’s server can’t start, the app’s window offers to restore the last scheduled backup; on another computer, a new Leafen’s first screen restores from the same backup place with “Restore it from a backup”.
restore.folderNewest: The command names the newest backup; for another, put its name from the backup folder’s Leafen backups/snapshots in its place.
restore.folderDownload: For backups on a WebDAV server or in S3, download the whole Leafen backups folder first and put where it is in the command.
restore.folderDownloadContainer: For backups on a WebDAV server or in S3, download the whole Leafen backups folder into the folder holding compose.yaml first.
restore.folderSealed: The backups are encrypted: give a file with the password on its first line to --password-file, or one with the recovery code to --recovery-code-file.
restore.folderSealedContainer: The backups are encrypted: put a file with the password on its first line in the folder holding compose.yaml and give it to --password-file, or one with the recovery code to --recovery-code-file.
restore.noSpace: This server’s disk has no room to put the backup together.

apps.title: Installed apps
apps.meta: Apps installed on this server. An app reaches people’s data and external addresses only within the permissions you approve.
apps.unsignedRefused: This server installs only signed apps, so it didn’t take this file. To install it, turn on “Allow unsigned app files” in the app policies below.
apps.packageTooLarge: This app file is bigger than the largest app file this server takes.
apps.uploadRefused: Leafen rejected the app file: something in it isn’t valid. Run leafen app validate in its folder to see what.

statusNote.stopped: It takes no new runs. Turn it on to use it again.
statusNote.emergency: Runs in progress were ended. Turn it on to use it again.

apps.removeConfirmBody: It stops on this server and is removed from the list.

review.title: Install {{name}}
review.updateFrom: The installed version is {{current}}; the new one is {{next}}.
review.reinstallFrom: This is the installed version, {{version}}, but its files differ. Reinstalling puts these files in place.
review.downgradeFrom: The installed version is {{current}}; this one, {{next}}, is earlier.
review.unchangedFrom: This is the same app as the installed version, {{version}}. Installing it would change nothing.
review.inTrash: This app is in Trash. Restore it from the list of apps, then update it.
review.permissionsChanged: What the app may do changed.
review.permissionsDetailsChanged: The list is the same, but details such as an action’s input or description changed, so it needs approval again.
review.permissionsSame: What the app may do is the same as the installed version’s.
review.permissionsDropped: What it may no longer do
review.nameLooksLike: Its name looks like {{name}}. Check that it’s really from who it claims before installing.
review.revoked: An app catalog revoked this version, so it can’t be installed. Upload another version. Reason: {{reason}}
review.needsLeafen: This app needs Leafen {{version}} or later, so this server can’t install it.
review.whoNote: You can change this any time in Settings → Server → Apps.
review.credentialsNote: Each person enters them in a Leafen window, and the app never sees them. Turn this off or revoke them all in Settings → Server → Apps.
review.noPermissions: It doesn’t access people’s data or external addresses
review.unreviewedWarning: I trust who made this app (no app catalog has reviewed it).
review.showAllPermissions: See everything this app may do

reading.fileLead: The file is uploaded to the server and its contents and permissions are checked. Then you’ll see what the app can do before you install it.
reading.catalogLead: The app is fetched from its catalog and its contents and permissions are checked. Then you’ll see what the app can do before you install it.

permission.personAccess_openedFile: Only the file a person opens with it, to read it and save it back
permission.personAccess_read: Read the pages the person using it can see
permission.personAccess_content: Read and edit what the person using it can edit
permission.personAccess_structure: Change pages, databases and their structure as far as the person using it can
permission.personAccess_admin: Act with an administrator’s rights when an administrator uses it
permission.directAddress: Connect directly to {{detail}} and exchange data with it
permission.relayAddress: Send requests to {{detail}} through this server
permission.privateNetwork: Reach {{detail}} on your private network through this server
permission.secret: Use the secret {{detail}} kept on this server
permission.outsideSignIn: Ask people to log in to {{detail}}
permission.realtime: Host live rooms of up to {{detail}} people
permission.webrtc: Connect people’s browsers to each other
permission.guests: Let people without an account join {{detail}} by link
permission.guestsCount_one: Let people without an account join {{count}} room by link
permission.guestsCount_other: Let people without an account join {{count}} rooms by link
permission.longRunningWorker: Keep the app’s server code running
permission.residentWorker: Keep the app’s server code loaded between its endpoints’ requests
permission.endpoint: Let programs outside Leafen log in with an app password at “{{detail}}” and act as far as the person may
permission.publicEndpoint: Let anyone reach “{{detail}}” without logging in (opens only once you allow it)
permission.storage: Keep up to {{detail}} of short-lived data
permission.lockedData: Keep data only the app may change ({{detail}})
permission.outsideSignInUse: Use an external login to connect: {{detail}}
permission.endpointPages: Serve its own web pages at “{{detail}}”: they run without an origin, so they can’t read Leafen’s login
permission.groups: Read your organization’s groups and which of the people who use it are in each
permission.notifications: Sends notices to the people who use it (inbox, mail and push)
permission.roomLoop: Keep the app’s server code running for each room while people are in it
permission.settingSocket: Keep a connection open to the {{detail}} the administrator sets
permission.personCredential: Ask people for their own {{detail}}, which Leafen stores encrypted
permission.credentialUse: Use a person’s account details to connect: {{detail}}
permission.credentialUseSetting: Use a person’s {{credential}} details to connect to the {{setting}} an administrator set
permission.webAssembly: Run WebAssembly in its screen, such as a document converter
permission.scriptEval: Run code its screen makes while it runs
permission.slashItemBlock: Adds a “/” menu item: {{name}} (adds the block “{{target}}”)
permission.menuActionTarget: Adds an item to the “…” menu of {{places}}: {{name}} (runs “{{target}}”)
permission.credentialUseTo: Use a person’s {{credential}} details to connect to {{where}}
permission.outsideSignInAt: Asks people to log in with {{provider}} ({{where}})
permission.directAddressFor: Connect directly to {{address}} and exchange data with it ({{kinds}})

removal.legalHold: A legal hold keeps this data, so it can’t be moved to Trash; it’s kept as ordinary workspaces.
removal.trash: Move the app and its data to Trash (deleted for good after {{days}} days)
removal.keep: Keep the data as ordinary workspaces

strict.title: Apps connect only through this server
strict.body: Apps connect to other sites through this server, never directly. Each connection is recorded.

homeScreen.title: Home screen apps
homeScreen.body: While an app is open, people can add it to their home screen or desktop as its own app with its name and icon.

unsigned.title: Allow unsigned app files
unsigned.body: Administrators can install app files without their developer’s signature after confirming they trust the developer. When off, only signed apps, apps from catalogs and built-in apps can be installed.

secrets.needsEntry: This server can’t open the saved value (it was encrypted with another key, as after a restore elsewhere). Enter it again.
secrets.meta: When the app connects to the addresses below, this server fills the value in. The app can’t see it, and only its last four characters show here.
secrets.callback: Register this redirect URI with each login provider:
secrets.returnMoved: The server’s address changed. Add the redirect URI above to {{provider}}’s OAuth client; until then, logins go through the earlier address {{earlier}}, which forwards here.
secrets.returnAdded: Logins with {{provider}} now use the new redirect URI, and this note disappears after the first one succeeds. If the provider rejects it, switch back to the earlier address.

hooks.needsNewSecret: This server can’t open the saved secret; calls are rejected until you create a new one.
hooks.title: Incoming webhooks
hooks.earlier: The last call came to the earlier address {{earlier}}, which forwards here: give the sender the address above.
hooks.verifyToken: Checked by a token in the address
hooks.empty: No secret yet: create one to accept calls
hooks.remakeConfirmDetail: Calls signed with the current secret are rejected until the sender has the new one.
hooks.once: This secret is shown only now. Paste it into the sending service.

orgs.title: Addresses for one organization — calls there run for it
orgs.removeConfirmDetail: Calls to it are rejected from then on
orgs.remakeConfirm: Create a new secret for this address?

jobs.title: {{name}} jobs
jobs.none: This app has no schedules or change triggers

status.halted: ended when the app was stopped

failure.busy: The app was too busy to run this
failure.workerStopped: The app’s runner stopped before it finished

guests.title: {{name}} guests
guests.body: People using the app can make a link that lets anyone in without logging in. Each room holds up to {{count}} guests. Guests use only that room and the app’s temporary storage, and don’t see any data.
guests.enabledBody: Off by default. Turning it off ends every guest’s session at once.
guests.revokeConfirmDetail: Guests who joined with it leave at once, and the link stops working.

browse.title: Browse apps
browse.noNetworkOnly: Only apps with no external connections
browse.noCatalogs: No catalogs are trusted yet. Add one in Manage catalogs.
browse.fetchFailed: Couldn’t fetch the app from its catalog

catalogs.title: App catalogs
catalogs.body: App catalogs this server trusts. A catalog is read only if it matches its developer’s key, and versions a catalog takes down stop wherever they’re installed.
catalogs.name: Catalog name
catalogs.uploadTitle: Add a catalog from a file (for a server without internet)
catalogs.addressRefused: The index address must start with https. An http address works only for this server’s own computer (localhost).
catalogs.unreachable: This server couldn’t read the catalog at that address. Check the address, and that this server can reach it.
catalogs.invalid: That catalog can’t be read or doesn’t match the key. Check the key and the address.

apps.pausedBudget: Stopped for calling Leafen too often for too long. Turn it on again once the app is fixed.

usage.title: {{name}} usage
usage.body: The last 24 hours. Calls to Leafen come from the app’s screen, its workers and agents using its tools.
usage.limitValue: {{calls}} calls and {{writes}} writes a minute for each person, and as many for the app itself
usage.endpointPersonStorage: Storage for each person (MiB, 0 for none of its own)
usage.endpointLimitsNote: By default {{perMinute}} a minute and {{concurrent}} at once, with no storage limit of the app’s own; the organization’s storage limit always applies.
usage.endpointPublicNote: The app declares this endpoint public. Once opened, anyone can reach the app at this address without logging in; an update that changes the app’s permissions closes it again.

policy.title: Who installs apps
policy.allowlistHint: Choose the apps people can add in <browse>Browse apps</browse>.

settings.title: {{name}} settings
settings.meta: The app connects to these addresses only, and only once you set them. Add a port after a colon if it isn’t the usual one.
settings.empty: Not set — the app can’t connect yet
settings.invalid: Enter a host name or IP address, with a port after a colon if needed.

credentials.title: People’s credentials
credentials.enabled: Let people give this app their credentials
credentials.meta: Each person enters theirs in a Leafen window; the app never sees it. People can remove theirs anytime.
credentials.revokeConfirmDetail: They’ll need to enter them again

data.title: What the update changes in the app’s data
data.kept: {{name}}: changed settings aren’t applied — people may have changed them
data.accept: What goes to Trash leaves the app’s data in every organization; people can restore it from Trash. I understand.
data.left: {{name}}: left as it is — the new version no longer uses it
data.leftRows: The rows the app put in {{name}}: left as they are
data.behind: {{line}} — where an earlier update didn’t finish

people.title: Who may use {{name}}
people.lead: Only the groups and people you check in {{tenancy}} may use the app; a group’s people change with the group. Checking everyone above covers them all.
people.readFailed: Couldn’t load the people and groups
people.more: Showing the first 100 — narrow the search

oversight.title: Approve every app action
oversight.body: Every app action in the organization asks a person first, and on the app’s screen no one can approve actions for an hour at a time.

apps.dataFailure: Couldn’t finish making this app’s data. It carries on the next time someone opens the app. Reason: {{reason}}
apps.dataUpdateFailure: Couldn’t finish bringing this app’s data up to the new version. It carries on the next time someone opens the app. Reason: {{reason}}
apps.personDataFailure_one: Couldn’t finish making one person’s own data for this app. It carries on the next time they use the app. Reason: {{reason}}
apps.personDataFailure_other: Couldn’t finish making {{count}} people’s own data for this app. It carries on the next time each of them uses the app. Reason: {{reason}}
apps.nobodyYet: No one can use this app yet. Choose who can below.

statusHint.stopped: Running work finishes, then the app stops.
statusHint.emergency: Running work is cut off and the app stops at once.

apps.restoredToast: Restored {{name}}. Turn it on to use it again.
apps.removeConfirmTrash: The app stops and moves to Trash. You can restore it within {{days}} days.

placeSearch.title: Place search
placeSearch.privacy: Off by default. Searches are sent from this server to the provider you configure. Addresses and credentials are stored encrypted and never returned to the browser.
placeSearch.environment: Server environment variables override or disable place search.
placeSearch.configured: Provider settings are saved. Empty fields keep the saved values.
placeSearch.keepStored: Leave empty to keep the saved value
placeSearch.manual: Search runs only when a person presses Search. Use a self-hosted or contracted Nominatim/Photon endpoint; the public OSMF Nominatim service is not supported. Kakao/NAVER use their official endpoint when the address is empty.

tunnel.title: Access from outside
tunnel.meta: Let people and agents outside your network (such as ChatGPT or Claude on the web) reach this server without a domain, port forwarding or certificate. Only administrators can turn it on.
tunnel.localOnly: At this address, this computer’s Leafen works like any server: devices you add, people you invite and agents connect there. It’s reachable only while this computer is on and awake.
tunnel.cloudflare: A quick tunnel or your own Cloudflare tunnel passes traffic through your free Cloudflare service, where it is decrypted.
tunnel.tailscaleDescription: Log in with your own Tailscale account and the server gets a fixed public https address. The free plan is for personal, non-commercial use, so a company needs a paid Tailscale plan.
tunnel.tailscaleSetup: Nothing to install. If you have no account, create one on Tailscale’s login page.
tunnel.tailscalePlan: Tailscale’s free plan is for personal, non-commercial use; a company needs its own paid Tailscale plan.
tunnel.ownAddressDescription: An https address your own reverse proxy or port forwarding already serves for this server. Leafen opens no tunnel and uses it everywhere.
tunnel.ownAddressFact: Connections reach your own proxy or this server directly; they are decrypted wherever your https ends.
tunnel.ownAddressTLS: (this server serves HTTPS itself on port {{port}})
tunnel.forwarding: The earlier address {{from}} forwards to {{to}} until {{date}}.
tunnel.forwardingProxy: It keeps working only while your own proxy or Cloudflare tunnel still routes it to this server.
tunnel.forwardingSignedOut: The earlier address {{from}} doesn’t forward now: its Tailscale device was logged out. To forward it again, switch the way to Tailscale, log in, then switch back to the current address.
tunnel.forwardingPaused: With access from outside off, the earlier address {{from}} doesn’t forward now; turned on again, it forwards until {{date}}.
tunnel.forwardingExtends: While it still receives requests, it stays for 30 days after the last one, up to a year from the change.
tunnel.tailscaleFact: Connections pass through Tailscale but are decrypted on this server. If a certificate for this address appears that this server didn’t request, the server finds it in the public certificate logs, notifies you and turns off the address.
tunnel.tailscaleLogin: Log in to Tailscale so Leafen gets its address. Any browser works, a phone’s too; Leafen notices when you’re done.
tunnel.tailscaleAllow: You’re logged in. Last, press “Open Tailscale” and allow Leafen’s address there; this screen moves on by itself once it’s allowed.
tunnel.tailscaleRenamed: Tailscale named this server differently because a device called “{{name}}” is still in your Tailscale. Remove that old device in Tailscale and turn this on again to get the same address.
tunnel.tailscalePublishing: Tailscale is putting Leafen’s address on the internet. The first time can take a few minutes.
tunnel.tailscaleTailnetName: The part after the first dot is your Tailscale network’s name. If you want another, change it in Tailscale’s DNS settings before you share links.
tunnel.certificateAlert: A certificate for this address that this server didn’t request appeared — issued by {{issuer}} on {{date}}. Someone could use it to decrypt connections Tailscale relays, so the public address was turned off.
tunnel.certificateAlertClear: It’s mine — turn the public address back on
tunnel.certificateWatchChecked: Last checked the public certificate logs for this address: {{date}}.
tunnel.certificateWatchUnverified: Couldn’t check the public certificate logs just now; trying again later. Last checked: {{date}}.
tunnel.configured: This server uses the address from its start settings (LEAFEN_PUBLIC_URL), {{address}}. Choose another way above and the server uses its address instead.
tunnel.configuredKept: The start settings (LEAFEN_PUBLIC_URL) still name {{address}}, but this server uses the address of the way chosen here.
tunnel.setByStart: This server’s start settings give its address (LEAFEN_PUBLIC_URL). To use another, remove it from the start settings and start the server again.
tunnel.offDescription: Reachable only from this computer or network.
tunnel.offReached: Leafen opens no way in itself, but this server was opened from outside at {{origin}}: a proxy or a router’s port forward in front of it serves it.
tunnel.quick: Try it for a while, no account
tunnel.quickDescription: A Cloudflare quick tunnel that opens in seconds with no account. Its address changes each time it starts.
tunnel.quickLimits: It takes up to 200 requests at once, with no guarantee.
tunnel.token: Keep using — your own Cloudflare tunnel
tunnel.tokenDescription: Enter the token of a tunnel you created in Cloudflare and the address its route serves. It reconnects automatically when the server starts.
tunnel.tokenKept: Set — enter only to change it

stage.approveDevice: Waiting for the tailnet’s admin to approve the device…
stage.allowFunnel: Waiting for the public address (HTTPS and Funnel) to be allowed…
stage.publishing: The address’s name is spreading through the public DNS…

tunnel.quickChanges: This address changes when you turn it off or on again. It’s temporary, so nothing carries over: reconnect agents that use it, and log in again in browsers at the new address.

failureKinds.program: The program that opens the address couldn’t be fetched or started. Leafen keeps trying; Details says why.
failureKinds.door: This server couldn’t open the way in for the tunnel. Leafen keeps trying; Details says why.
failureKinds.stopped: The address hasn’t opened yet, and Leafen keeps trying. If this network blocks it, choose another way.
failureKinds.token: The tunnel’s token can’t be read. Enter it again.
failureKinds.publicAddress: Tailscale hasn’t opened the public address yet, and Leafen keeps trying. If it keeps failing, choose another way.
failureKinds.certificateElsewhere: A certificate for this address was issued somewhere else, so the address stays off until an administrator confirms it’s theirs.
failureKinds.ownAddress: HTTPS on your own address isn’t running: its certificate can’t be read, or its port can’t be taken. Leafen keeps trying; Details says why.
failureKinds.noTailscale: Tailscale isn’t part of Leafen on phones. Use it on a server that stays on.
failureKinds.heldMoved: This server’s data moved to another server, which now answers at this address.
failureKinds.heldWaiting: This server opens its address once it confirms it still holds its data; its standby may have taken over.
failureKinds.heldReplicaUnreachable: This server can’t reach its replica, so its address waits for the standby, or for the replica to answer again.
failureKinds.unknown: The address isn’t open. Details says why.

tunnel.tokenInvalid: Check the tunnel’s token and its address, which starts with https://.
tunnel.addressInvalid: Enter an address that starts with https://, such as https://wiki.example.com
tunnel.door: In Cloudflare, set this tunnel’s service to {{address}}. Only requests through that port are trusted to carry each person’s own IP address.
tunnel.doorMissed: The tunnel connects to the server’s main port instead of its tunnel port, so each person’s IP address can’t be known and request limits apply to everyone together. In Cloudflare, change the service to {{address}}.
tunnel.tailscaleLoginOpened: Tailscale’s login is open in your browser. Log in and Leafen gets its address; this screen moves on by itself.
tunnel.tailscaleAllowOpened: Tailscale’s page to allow Leafen’s address is open. Allow it there and this screen moves on by itself.

unenforcedPolicies.notice: This server runs without the organization module, so the organization policies in its data aren’t enforced: {{policies}}. Nothing is permanently deleted while a legal hold is active. Run the full Leafen build to enforce them.

policy.passwordTwoStep: Password and 2-step verification instead of device codes

workspaceContent.notice: You’re viewing this as a server administrator. What you open or change here is recorded, and this workspace’s owner sees it.

pages.choose: Choose a page to read it here
pages.truncated: Only the beginning of this long page is shown.
pages.trashMessage: Move the page {{title}} and its sub-pages to Trash?
pages.trashDetail: The owner can restore them from Trash.
pages.deleteMessage: Permanently delete the page {{title}} and its sub-pages?
pages.held: It’s under a legal hold and can’t be deleted.
pages.deleting: Still deleting. Press it again to continue.
pages.rowHint: A database item is deleted with its database’s page.
pages.takeOverDetail: The person this page belonged to left the workspace, so no one can change who has it. The owner gets full access and can decide its sharing again. Everyone else keeps their access, and this goes in the server administrator record below.
pages.takenOver: The owner now has full access to this page.

files.inUseHint: It’s deleted when the page it’s on is deleted.
files.historyOnlyHint: No page uses this file now; only pages’ version history points to it. Deleting it frees its space, and those versions show the file as gone.
files.deleteHistoryOnlyDetail: Only pages’ version history keeps this file. Once deleted, those versions can’t open it either, and this can’t be undone.

public.disableDetail: Its public address stops working immediately

log.title: Server administrator log
log.description: Server administrators can see every workspace on the server. This is what they opened or changed in this workspace.

replication.title: Continuous replication
replication.toggle: Send every change to the backup location within seconds
replication.help: Database changes are sent every second and new files within seconds, to the same location as the backups. If this server is lost, another server pointed at that location can restore from it, a few seconds behind. Encrypted with the backup password if one is set.
replication.ownedElsewhere: Another server’s replica is at this location. Restore from it in Restore and move, or choose another location.
replication.moved: This server’s data moved to another server that was restored from the replica. Changes here aren’t kept.
replication.movedTo: This server’s data moved to {{address}}, which was restored from the replica. Changes here aren’t kept.
replication.keepApart: Use this server on its own
replication.keepApartHelp: It accepts changes again as a separate server, with replication off, so it never writes to the other server’s replica. Changes made on the other server don’t come here.
replication.missing: The replica this server wrote isn’t at the backup location any more (the location is empty, or another one is mounted there). Turn replication off and on to start it again.
replication.needsBackup: Continuous replication goes where scheduled backups go. Turn those on first.

standby.title: Standby server
standby.newCodeMade: Made a new code. Earlier codes no longer work.
standby.addHelp: A second Leafen server follows this one through the replica and takes over automatically if this one stops responding. It needs the same version or newer. With the Tailscale address, the server that takes over responds at the same address. With your own domain, point the domain to the server that took over; with a quick tunnel, the address changes after a takeover.
standby.codeHelp: Paste it on the other server under Settings → Server → Standby server → Become a standby server. It contains the backup location’s keys and password: give it only to that server’s administrator. Making a new code stops earlier codes that haven’t been used. If a code went somewhere it shouldn’t, also change the backup location’s keys there and enter the new keys in the backup location here.
standby.primaryHelp: If this server can’t reach the backup location for 10 seconds, it stops accepting changes until it can, so the standby can take over safely.
standby.paused: This server can’t reach the backup location, so it isn’t accepting changes now; the standby may take over.
standby.following: This server follows {{address}} and takes over when it stops responding.
standby.followingPlace: This server follows the primary through the backup location and takes over when the primary stops responding.
standby.takingOver: Taking over… the server restarts shortly
standby.auto: Take over automatically when the primary doesn’t respond for 30 seconds
standby.takeOverQuestion: Take over as the primary now?
standby.takeOverWarning: This server takes over from the replica and restarts as the primary. If the old primary is still running, it stops accepting changes.
standby.help: To update the pair with only a moment’s pause: update this standby first, take over, then update the old primary and add it as the new standby.
standby.joinHelp: This server’s own data is replaced by the primary’s when it takes over.
standby.tookOverPrimary: Took over from the primary at {{time}}
standby.codeInvalid: This connection code can’t be used. Make a new one on the primary server and paste it.
standby.notFresh: This server replicates its own data; turn that off first.
standby.versionOlder: This server is older than the primary; update it first.
standby.replicaUnavailable: The primary’s replica isn’t at that location, or the password doesn’t open it.
standby.earlierLeafen: The primary’s data is from an earlier Leafen, which this version doesn’t open, so this standby doesn’t take over. Move the primary’s workspaces one by one to a server on this version instead: on that server, make a new workspace and start it with “Move from another server”, then paste its code in the primary’s workspace settings, under Move this workspace.

direct.unreachable: Not reachable — judged by the backup location alone
direct.none: No address — judged by the backup location alone

standby.placeSlow: A standby needs a backup location both servers can access at the same time, such as S3 or a shared drive. A cloud sync folder shows changes too late.
standby.meta: If this server stops, another server takes over from a few seconds before.
standby.addNeedsReplication: To give this server a standby, turn on continuous replication above first. Below is for making this server another server’s standby.

remoteChoice.title: Open Leafen from anywhere?
remoteChoice.configuredTitle: This server uses the address from its start settings
remoteChoice.configuredBody: Links, invitations and agent connections use this address. Choose another way and its address is used instead.
remoteChoice.body: For your phone, people you work with and AI apps on the internet to get into Leafen, it needs an internet address of its own.
remoteChoice.phone: A phone’s own Leafen stops when the app closes, so it opens no public address. To reach it from outside, move it to a computer or server that stays on.
remoteChoice.tailscaleSteps: Log in with a free Tailscale account and allow it, and you’re done. Nothing to install.
remoteChoice.tailscaleFact: Connections pass through Tailscale but are decrypted on this server.
remoteChoice.domainBody: An address you already have, a Cloudflare tunnel of your own, or port forwarding.
remoteChoice.directHint: For a company’s server, or one that already has a way in from outside (port forwarding or your own domain), <way>Use my own domain</way> is recommended.
remoteChoice.quick: Try it for a while, no account
remoteChoice.quickBody: A Cloudflare quick tunnel: the address changes each time it starts, which breaks connected agents and shared links.
remoteChoice.laterBody: Leave it as it is; you’ll be asked again when something needs an address.
remoteChoice.signInQRAlt: QR code of the Tailscale login address
remoteChoice.allowQRAlt: QR code of Tailscale’s page that allows the public address
remoteChoice.quickFailing: The tunnel hasn’t opened yet, and it keeps trying. If this network blocks it, go back and choose another way.
remoteChoice.tailscaleFailing: Tailscale hasn’t opened the address yet, and it keeps trying. If it keeps failing, go back and choose another way.
remoteChoice.addressQR: Scan with your phone to log in there
remoteChoice.addressQRAlt: QR code of this server’s public address
remoteChoice.quickChanges: A quick tunnel’s address changes each time it starts.
remoteChoice.ownTitle: Make an address of your own
remoteChoice.closedBody: This server can’t reach the internet, so it’s opened at a company address with the company’s certificate.
remoteChoice.ownBody: This server can reach the internet but can’t use Tailscale ({{reason}}). Set up an address of your own with an agent.
remoteChoice.handToAgentBody: Copies a prompt with what this server detected. The agent explains the options and asks before each change that affects the network, security or cost.
remoteChoice.handToAgentClosed: Copies a prompt for setting it up at a company address with the company’s certificate, to work through with your IT team.
remoteChoice.handToAgentCopied: Copied. Paste it into your agent; this window detects when the address is set.
remoteChoice.doItYourselfBody: The guide: port forwarding, IPv6, a VPS with frp, a domain.
remoteChoice.doItYourselfClosed: The guide: a company address, its certificate, a reverse proxy.

reasons.intercepted: something in between intercepts the encrypted connection, such as a company proxy

check.ok: Checked: a certificate for {{names}}, until {{date}}. Open it on your phone.
check.dns: Checked: this address’s name doesn’t resolve yet. Check its DNS record.
check.unreachable: Checked: nothing answers HTTPS at this address yet. Check the proxy, port forwarding or firewall.
check.name: Checked: the certificate answering at this address is for another name.
check.expired: Checked: the certificate answering at this address has expired.
check.untrusted: Checked: this computer doesn’t trust the certificate’s issuer, and devices that don’t trust it refuse it too.

prompt.closedIntro: Help me give my Leafen server an address people in my company can open. Leafen measured that this server doesn’t reach the internet, so it is on a closed network: use a company address and the company’s certificate.
prompt.ownIntro: Help me give my Leafen server an address that works from outside. It can’t use Tailscale here, so we make one of our own, together.
prompt.factsTitle: What Leafen measured on this server:
prompt.factPortMapping: - Router opens ports by itself: NAT-PMP {{natpmp}}, UPnP {{upnp}}
prompt.closedWays: Options to consider: an internal DNS name for this server, the company’s certificate or its internal CA, and a reverse proxy the IT team already runs, or Leafen serving HTTPS itself with that certificate.
prompt.ownWays: Options to consider: port forwarding on the router (or its automatic port opening above), the global IPv6 address, a small VPS with frp, a tunnel service that works where I am, and a domain name. Weigh what each costs, what it exposes and how long it lasts.
prompt.consult: Work it out with me: tell me what you found and the ways open, with their trade-offs, and let me choose. Ask me before each change that touches the network, security or money (router or firewall settings, installing a program, buying a VPS or a domain), and make it only after I agree.
prompt.safety: Rules: HTTPS only. Never open Leafen’s admin pages without login. Don’t turn off security settings.
prompt.finish: Last, don’t edit files by hand: call the Leafen MCP tool leafen_remote_access with action set_address and the https address, plus certificate, key and port when this server should take HTTPS itself. It works only on an admin connection. Leafen checks the address and shows me a QR to open it on my phone.
prompt.connectFirst: First connect to my Leafen as its administrator (Settings → Features → Agents gives the text), so you can use its tools.
prompt.companyIntro: Help me give my Leafen server an address people in my company can open. It belongs to a company, so use the company’s own domain and certificate rather than a personal Tailscale address; work out with me where it fits in the company’s network.

remoteChoice.companyBody: This looks like a company’s server (a company mail domain or an organization’s domain), so it opens at the company’s own address and certificate first. Tailscale’s free plan isn’t for business use, and company networks often block it.
remoteChoice.tailscaleAtCompany: Its free plan is for personal use; a company needs a paid plan, and some company networks block it.
remoteChoice.skipCost: If you skip this, phones and AI apps on the internet can’t get in. You can turn it on later in Settings.

serverMove.title: Move to another server
serverMove.meta: Everything moves: people, pages, history, files, settings and the remote address.
serverMove.confirmQuestion: Move this server to the new server?
serverMove.outHelp: On the new server, open Settings → Server → Restore and move → Move a server here, and paste its code here. The new server needs this version or newer.
serverMove.warning: From now on no one can make changes here, and the remote address moves to the new server. This server stays read-only and points there; “Use this server on its own” restores it.
serverMove.copying: Sending everything to {{address}}… No one can make changes here meanwhile.
serverMove.finishing: {{address}} is verifying and restoring the data; it restarts with this server’s data.
serverMove.movedOut: This server’s data moved to {{address}}. It no longer accepts changes here.
serverMove.failed: The move stopped, and this server accepts changes again as before. To try again, paste the same code again. If it isn’t taken, create a new one on the new server.
serverMove.inEarlierLeafen: The other server’s data is from an earlier Leafen, which this version doesn’t take, so nothing was moved. Move its workspaces over one by one instead: make a new workspace here and start it with “Move from another server”, then paste its code in the other server’s workspace settings, under Move this workspace.
serverMove.inRefused: The other server’s data can’t be opened here, so nothing was moved.
serverMove.inHelp: Creates a code valid for an hour. Everything on this server is replaced with the other server’s; current data is kept aside for 7 days.
serverMove.inNotEmpty: Other people use this server. A whole server moves only to one no one else uses yet; move a workspace instead.
serverMove.inCodeLabel: Code for the server that moves here
serverMove.inCodeHelp: Paste it on the old server under Settings → Server → Restore and move → Move this server, before {{time}}. It lets only that server connect here: don’t share it.
serverMove.inStoppedIncomplete: Receiving stopped: what was sent didn’t all arrive, or doesn’t match its list.
serverMove.inStoppedBusy: Receiving stopped: a backup or restore was running on this server.
serverMove.inStoppedFailed: Receiving stopped: this server couldn’t put together the data that arrived. Check the server’s log.
serverMove.inStoppedNext: Nothing changed on this server. To try again, paste the same code on the old server again; to stop, cancel.
serverMove.restoring: Restoring the data; this server restarts with it in a moment.
serverMove.restoringManual: Restored. Quit Leafen and open it again to start with the moved data.
serverMove.movedInHelp: Switch your apps and phones to this server’s address, and give outside agents the connection text under Settings → Features → Agents. Check the backup settings: a backup folder may not exist on this computer.
serverMove.codeInvalid: The new server doesn’t take this code. It may have expired, or the new server restarted and no longer has it. Create a new one on the new server.
serverMove.versionOlder: The new server is older than this one. Update it first.
serverMove.unreachable: This server couldn’t reach the new server at the address in the code.
serverMove.busy: This server is moving, restoring or backing up now. Try again when it’s done.
serverMove.sameServer: That code is this server’s own. Paste it on the server that moves here.

general.meta: This server’s name and what it holds.

backupOff.settings: Scheduled backups are off. This server’s pages and files are on it alone, and nothing brings them back if its disk fails.
